status_summary: Executive Order 14321 (2025-07-24) directed HUD and HHS to end support for Housing First policies and to raise treatment requirements, and HUD has pursued this through Continuum of Care funding notices rather than a change to 24 CFR part 578 or a statute. After the Rhode Island district court vacated HUD's November and December 2025 notices on 2026-06-29 (per its later opinion), HUD's FY2026 notice of 2026-06-01 offered about $4.04 billion, set aside about $1.3 billion for new transitional-housing and services-only projects and added scoring points for treatment and required supportive services, according to the Congressional Research Service. The district court set that notice aside on 2026-08-07 for lack of notice and comment; the First Circuit stayed that ruling on 2026-09-16, HUD reopened the notice on 2026-09-18 with applications due 2026-09-30, and on 2026-09-24 the First Circuit vacated the district court judgment and remanded after construing plaintiffs to have waived the notice-and-comment claim, without ruling on the merits. On 2026-11-03 HUD published a notice of waiver (91 FR 69267) of the 30-day minimum application period for the FY2026 notice that reopened on 2026-09-18. Plaintiffs' other claims remain pending in the district court, and HUD's competition page lists no FY2026 awards as of 2026-11-03.

timeline.event: Executive Order 14321 signed; Section 5 directs HUD and HHS to end support for Housing First policies and HUD to increase treatment requirements for participants with substance use disorder or serious mental illness.

A state coalition sues over HUD's FY2025 Continuum of Care notice (issued in November 2025, which de-emphasized Housing First); a separate suit by cities and nonprofits follows on 2025-12-01. A court enters a preliminary injunction in December 2025 and HUD withdraws and later reopens the prior-year notice.

HUD announces the first round of FY2025 Continuum of Care renewal awards ($349 million for 622 projects); later rounds follow on 2026-04-27 and 2026-05-21, totaling about $3.85 billion, under the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (Public Law 119-75).

The First Circuit (Nos. 26-1217 and 26-1218, consolidated) denies HUD's motion for a stay pending its appeal of the Rhode Island district court's denial of HUD's motion to dissolve the December 2025 preliminary injunctions on the FY2025 notice, finding HUD had not shown the district court abused its discretion; HUD had not appealed the 2025-12-23 injunction orders themselves. JURIST reports HUD had not announced whether it would appeal further.
timeline.source: U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit (copy hosted by justsecurity.org); JURIST

timeline.event: HUD issues the FY2026 Continuum of Care NOFO: about $4.04 billion total, about $1.3 billion (roughly 30 percent) set aside for new transitional-housing and services-only projects, 60 percent of annual renewal demand available in tier 1 (the statutory minimum), and scoring points for treatment and recovery services and for requiring participation in supportive services (CRS). A lawsuit follows on 2026-07-02 and HUD modifies the notice on 2026-07-24.

D.R.I. Judge Mary McElroy rules HUD's 2025 overhaul of the program violated the Administrative Procedure Act and vacates HUD's November and December 2025 NOFOs (per the court's 2026-08-07 background); she declines to bar similar future changes or to fold the FY2026 notice into the same case (Maryland Matters).

Judge McElroy (State of Washington v. HUD, 1:26-cv-00439; NAEH v. HUD, 1:26-cv-00436) grants summary judgment in part and sets aside the FY2026 NOFO in its entirety: the roughly $1.3 billion set-aside requires notice and comment under 42 U.S.C. 11386b(d)(2)(C), which HUD did not provide; the court denies a permanent injunction against future versions, does not reach the other challenges (including OMB apportionment footnotes) and does not rule on whether the policy shift from Housing First is lawful on its merits. HUD appeals on 2026-08-13.
timeline.source: U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island (via govinfo)

timeline.event: The First Circuit (Nos. 26-1922 and 26-1923, consolidated) grants HUD a stay pending appeal of the district court's 2026-08-07 set-aside. The order finds HUD likely to succeed on the argument that the roughly $1.3 billion set-aside is not a bonus or other incentive under 42 U.S.C. 11386b(d), and finds irreparable injury to HUD from its 2026-12-01 deadline for Continuum of Care awards.
timeline.source: U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit (via Justia)

timeline.event: HUD reopens the FY2026 Continuum of Care NOFO, citing the First Circuit's 2026-09-16 stay, with applications due 2026-09-30.

Plaintiffs in National Alliance to End Homelessness v. HUD (1st Cir. No. 26-1923) file an emergency motion asking the First Circuit to vacate the district court's set-aside summarily and remand for their remaining claims, with the mandate to issue at once, or alternatively to expedite the appeal for decision before 2026-12-01; they state they are willing to forgo the 42 U.S.C. 11386b(d) notice-and-comment claim. The motion says HUD will endeavor to make awards by the statutory deadline of 2026-12-01 and notes HUD reopened the notice on 2026-09-18 (see 2026-09-24).
timeline.source: U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit filing (copy hosted by endhomelessness.org)

timeline.event: The First Circuit enters judgment vacating the district court's judgment and remanding both appeals for further proceedings. The panel construes plaintiffs, who had moved for summary vacatur and remand, to have waived the statutory notice-and-comment claim on which the district court judgment rested, finds no live dispute on appeal, holds plaintiffs estopped from raising that claim again and expects any later district judgment to dismiss it with prejudice; it does not rule on the merits of the set-aside. The judgment states the mandate issues the same day. Plaintiffs' remaining challenges return to the district court.

title: End Housing First requirements and shift homelessness funding toward treatment first
uncertainties: Sources conflict on what HUD did in December 2025: a law-firm summary says a preliminary injunction required HUD to keep the prior-year NOFO and HUD reopened it in January 2026 (the California Attorney General's press release of 2026-06-29 does not state this), while Smart Cities Dive describes a December reissue with similar policy changes and Maryland Matters reports a new NOFO on 2025-12-19; the Rhode Island court's 2026-08-07 opinion says its 2026-06-29 order vacated both the November and December 2025 notices, but the 2025 and June 2026 orders themselves were not read. The First Circuit's opinion of 2026-04-01 (Nos. 26-1217 and 26-1218, read on a copy hosted by justsecurity.org) denies HUD's motion for a stay pending its appeal of the district court's refusal to dissolve the December 2025 preliminary injunctions and notes that HUD did not appeal the 2025-12-23 injunction orders themselves; JURIST (2026-04-02), the San Francisco City Attorney (2026-04-01) and Scotsman Guide describe the same denial, and JURIST says HUD had not announced whether it would appeal further. The California Attorney General's press release of 2026-06-29 says HUD abandoned that appeal in April 2026; no court document or news report confirming the abandonment was found, so it is an unverified lead at low confidence. The 2026-08-07 district order (on govinfo and in a copy posted by the New York Attorney General), the 2026-09-16 First Circuit stay order (Justia) and the 2026-09-24 First Circuit judgment (a copy posted by plaintiffs' counsel, the ACLU of Rhode Island) were opened and read; no copy of the judgment on a court site, govinfo or courtlistener was located. The judgment rests on waiver by plaintiffs and does not decide the merits of the set-aside; the stay order's merits view is preliminary. The judgment states the mandate issues on 2026-09-24, while the district docket as mirrored by the Civil Rights Litigation Clearinghouse lists a mandate entry on 2026-09-28; the later date was not checked against an opened copy and may be a docketing date. The 2026-12-01 award deadline comes from the stay order, not from HUD's program page, which states no award date. The district court's 2026-09-29 briefing schedule and 2026-10-16 notice (ECF 54) are known only from the docket mirror, the supplemental briefs were not read, and no district court ruling on the remaining claims was found as of 2026-10-22. A separate HUD Federal Register notice on incentivized homelessness-reduction activities (comments due 2026-10-13) was not read. No rule change to 24 CFR part 578 and no statute was located. As context only, the House Appropriations Committee reported the FY2027 THUD bill (H.R. 9170) on 2026-06-05 with about $4.16 billion for Homeless Assistance Grants, against $4.42 billion enacted for FY2026 and a $4.02 billion request (CRS); CRS describes no Housing First or treatment conditions, the bill's homeless assistance paragraph was not read, and the bill has not passed the House. The 2026-11-03 waiver notice (91 FR 69267-69268, FR-6570-N-02, docket HUD-2025-0704) was read in its Federal Register API record only; its full text was not read for any Housing First or treatment content, and it names no signer by name or signing date in that record. It addresses the shortened application period of the reopened notice and shows no change in the notice's substance. HUD's competition page, read on hud.gov on 2026-11-03, still lists no FY2026 awards.
